passages.t: God summons his people: ‘I have no need for a bull from your stall’
passages.happening:
The heading reads, “A Psalm of Asaph” (verse 1). The book page says who Asaph was: a leader of the temple singers.

The psalm opens like a court being called to order. “The Mighty One, God the LORD, speaks and summons the earth from where the sun rises to where it sets” (verse 1). He comes from Zion in fire and storm (verses 2 and 3). Heaven and earth are called as witnesses, “that He may judge His people” (verse 4).

Then God speaks to his own people. He does not complain about their worship. “I do not rebuke you for your sacrifices, and your burnt offerings are ever before Me” (verse 8). But he does not need it. “I have no need for a bull from your stall or goats from your pens” (verse 9). Every beast is his already, “the cattle on a thousand hills” (verse 10). “If I were hungry, I would not tell you, for the world is Mine, and the fullness thereof” (verse 12).

What he wants is this. “Sacrifice a thank offering to God, and fulfill your vows to the Most High. Call upon Me in the day of trouble; I will deliver you, and you will honor Me” (verses 14 and 15).
passages.hearers:
Israel's worship centred on sacrifice. In a burnt offering the whole animal was burned. In a thank offering, part was burned and the family ate the rest in a happy meal, giving thanks for God's help (Leviticus 7:12). A vow was a promise, often made in danger, to give God something when he answered.

Many peoples around Israel thought their gods needed feeding. Sacrifice was a way of keeping a god fed and on your side. Psalm 50 laughs at that idea. “Do I eat the flesh of bulls, or drink the blood of goats?” (verse 13).

Calling heaven and earth as witnesses was the language of a covenant, a binding agreement. The prophets used this courtroom picture when God brought charges against his people.
passages.later:
The prophets say the same thing in sharp words. “For I desire mercy, not sacrifice, and the knowledge of God rather than burnt offerings” (Hosea 6:6). Micah asks, “what does the LORD require of you but to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God?” (Micah 6:8).

The letter to the Hebrews takes up the thank offering: “Through Jesus, therefore, let us continually offer to God a sacrifice of praise, the fruit of lips that confess His name” (Hebrews 13:15).
passages.hard: If God did not want sacrifices, why did he command them? The psalm does not reject sacrifice. Verse 8 says so plainly. What it rejects is the idea that God needs it, and the habit of offering it while living as if God did not matter. Most readers take the prophets' sharp words in the same way: God wants mercy more than sacrifice, not sacrifice without mercy. Some scholars read them as a deeper criticism of sacrifice itself. Either way, the gift was always for Israel's good, a way to draw near, and never a meal God needed.
passages.asks:
God does not need anything from you. That can sound cold, but it is freeing. You cannot keep God going with your religion. What he asks for is thanks, honesty and prayer: ‘Call upon Me in the day of trouble.’

What are you giving God as if he needed it? What would it look like to thank him instead?

passages.t: ‘What right have you to recite My statutes?’
passages.happening:
Now God speaks to a different group. “To the wicked, however, God says, ‘What right have you to recite My statutes and to bear My covenant on your lips?’” (verse 16).

These people know the words. They can quote God's law. But “you hate My instruction and cast My words behind you” (verse 17). They make friends with thieves and adulterers (verse 18). They use their tongues for lies and slander their own brothers (verses 19 and 20).

God had been silent, and they took it wrongly. God says, “you thought I was just like you. But now I rebuke you and accuse you to your face” (verse 21).

The warning is fierce (verse 22). But the last word is an open door. “He who sacrifices a thank offering honors Me, and to him who rights his way, I will show the salvation of God” (verse 23).
passages.hearers:
The charges come straight from the Ten Commandments: stealing, adultery and false witness. These were people at worship, saying the right words. The psalm shows that God hears the words and watches the life.

‘I kept silent’ (verse 21) is a sharp line. When God does not punish at once, people may think he does not care, or that he is like them. The psalm says his silence was patience, not approval.
passages.later: Jesus quoted Isaiah against religion that is only on the lips: “These people honor Me with their lips, but their hearts are far from Me” (Mark 7:6). Paul writes that God's kindness is meant to lead people to repent (Romans 2:4).
passages.asks:
This part is not for ‘the wicked’ out there. It is for people who know their Bibles. It is possible to quote God and ignore him.

But notice how it ends. It does not close the door. Anyone who ‘rights his way’, who turns, will see God's salvation. If the silence of God has made you careless, this is your warning, and it is also your invitation.
